data.title: In search of Roman remains in Africa – Carthage and Pupput
data.excerpt: A journey after the Roman remains of North Africa. Carthage, founded according to legend by the princess Elyssa and famous for the baths of Antoninus Pius, and the little-known Roman town of Pupput near Hammamet, whose mosaics lie largely unexcavated and unprotected.
data.metaTitle: Roman remains in Africa – Carthage and Pupput
data.metaDescription: A journey after the Roman remains of Tunisia: Carthage with the baths of Antoninus Pius, and the little-known town of Pupput near Hammamet.

mediaTexts.alt: A map of the Mediterranean in 218 BC with the empires and the sites of battles marked in colour

children.text: Thousands of years before our generation, the Mediterranean Sea was surrounded by three continents. We may regard it as the cradle of the peoples, empires and civilisations that occupied, ruled and shaped it. Seen in this way, the Mediterranean is both a common factor and a common denominator of countless indigenous cultures, a meeting place of the civilisations of East and West, of Europe, Asia and Africa. It was the inland sea of great empires, between which various relations were built up; these places were linked by sea routes that formed a network of trading towns. The traffic between them moved not only goods, materials and artefacts, but also all sorts of people… some of them peaceable, others less so… merchants, soldiers, travellers, pilgrims… they carried with them their wares, their weapons, their knowledge, their experience, their faith… and in some such poetic way we can begin the adventure of the Phoenicians.

Present-day Tunisia, with its capital Tunis, lies precisely on the territory of ancient Carthage. The country gained independence from French colonial rule in 1956. In mid-December 2010 social unrest broke out in the country, which at the beginning of January 2011 grew into armed clashes with the police and the army. Even today the outcome of these clashes is visible in the streets of the towns, and people’s memories are still vivid. The subsequent overthrow of the ruler, President Ben Ali, on 14 January 2011 began a wave of revolutions (in Tunisia the revolution was given the epithet “jasmine”), known in the other Arab countries as the “Arab Spring”. These facts and their consequences can still be felt as you travel through the country. What is positive, however, is the effort to improve things, and it is clear that such a change in the right direction has already begun. The ongoing construction of roads, motorways and modern buildings is admittedly only in its beginnings, but one has to start somewhere. A modern cultural centre has been built in the centre of the capital, Tunis; the food in the restaurant there was excellent and the waiters very friendly… but for us Europeans it is slightly below the standard we have grown used to in recent years. In Tunis it is worth visiting the bazaar, the so-called medina, where the traders offer their wares. Clothes, perfumes, leather goods, jewellery, spices, all kinds of accessories, embroidered cushions, sweets… and all of it with a style of its own and a feel for haggling over the price. In the words of one of them: this is my shop, where I set the price; you tell me the price you are willing to buy at, and if I like your offer, we shall find common ground. In 2011 the first democratic elections were held in Tunisia, won by a party of moderate Islamists. On 12 December 2011 parliament elected a new interim president, Moncef Marzouki. Today the country has 17% unemployment and as much as 35% illiteracy. This autumn elections will be held in Tunisia which, all the locals believe, will help to improve the situation. When we consider what a glorious history Carthage has, how the insights into seafaring and shipbuilding were of unheard-of scope, how the cultural influence of ancient Greece and Rome is still palpable here, how highly accomplished the Arab scholars were and what a powerful idea Indian mathematics, medicine, astronomy and physics represented, it is surprising what level of education is found in this very part of North Africa today. The long-standing Arab influence brought Arabic as the official language; the majority religion is Muslim…

children.text: Carthage has many epithets. Carthage is a ship at anchor. The queen of the sea. The mistress of a maritime empire. All these comparisons are connected with the sea. The city of Carthage, as is well known, was founded by seafarers from the city of Tyre (Tyros – today Sour in present-day Lebanon). Throughout the whole period of its existence Carthage was a citadel that was the goal of many, and its inhabitants looked proudly from its walls towards the most distant horizons. According to legend it was the princess Elyssa, who came from Tyre, who founded the new city on African soil… and so Elyssa and her followers finally reached the shores of Africa. They sought friendship with the native people, who saw in their arrival the chance of profitable trade. Princess Elyssa wanted to buy land, but the Berber ruler refused. Elyssa asked only for a piece of land as large as an oxhide would cover, so that she and her companions could rest after the exhausting voyage at sea. The Africans were probably afraid that the strangers might settle in large numbers in their neighbourhood, but this proposal seemed modest to them and they accepted it. They did not reckon with the trick Elyssa had devised. She had the oxhide cut into thin strips, and so she managed to cover a wider area than the natives could have imagined at first sight. The hill on which Carthage arose is called Byrsa – which in Greek means “oxhide”.

children.text: Directly below the hill lay one of the most important points – the harbour. This harbour is interesting and beautiful even today; how much more imposing it must have been at the height of its fame. But about this harbour and its shipyard, perhaps another time.

Carthage was a metropolis on the territory of present-day Tunis. In antiquity Carthage was at first the capital of the maritime and trading power of the same name. The Romans called the inhabitants “Punics”, a name derived from the designation “Quart hadasht” used by the Phoenicians, which means “new city”. The name Phoenicia, on the other hand, is derived from the Greek word “phoenike”, which means “purple land”. The Latin “poeni” probably comes from there. The history of the Carthaginian empire covers the development of the ancient maritime power from the founding of the city of Carthage, which existed between 825 and 814/813 BC. The fame of Phoenician ships passed also to the ships of Carthage; famous Carthaginian navigators recorded on maps the routes that opened the way westwards for people. Hanno (* before 480 BC; † c. 440 BC), also called Hanno the Navigator, was a Carthaginian admiral who lived around 470 BC. He probably sailed along the west African coast to the Gulf of Guinea with the aim of opening new trade routes. His account of the voyage (the Periplus) has come down to us in a Greek translation. The name Hanno was quite common in ancient Carthage; the identification of the navigator with other figures of the same name mentioned in other sources is therefore uncertain and disputed, especially because Hanno’s account of the voyage gives no important dates. Hanno may have been a navigator roughly between 480 and 440 BC, as the successor and son of Hamilcar, the ruler of Carthage. In the Periplus Hanno is referred to as βασιλεύς basileus, which probably indicates the office of suffete, a high dignitary in the Carthaginian state, though this is attested with certainty only around 410.

children.text: After the destruction of Carthage by the Romans in 146 BC, this territory was incorporated into the Roman Empire.

as Marcus Porcius Cato remarked many times at sessions of the senate. After his visit to Carthage this respected member of the senate was astonished and literally alarmed by the renewed prosperity of Rome’s former enemy, and so he constantly called for its destruction. Most of today’s ruins originate from Roman Carthage, which was founded on the site by Gaius Julius Caesar on the ruins of the older city and soon grew again into a beautiful and important city, in which busy life and thriving trade pulsed until the end of antiquity. From Punic times there is today a Punic necropolis on the hill of Byrsa, and the path to it is lined with small stone sarcophagi. Today Carthage is a suburb of the capital, Tunis. The archaeological site of Carthage has been on the UNESCO list since 1979. Carthage is enchanting in its history, and the splendour of the baths of the emperor Antoninus Pius still recalls its bygone glory. These baths, or rather the ruins, the remains of the foundations of the Baths of Antoninus, are at present the greatest attraction. They were built around 160 with an area of about 18,000 m², and on the northern side they are today enclosed by the presidential palace.

children.text: Africa, however, is full of surprises, and I should like to draw attention to the Roman town of Pupput, which is less well known, but whose beauty appealed to me. Pupput, also spelled “Putput”, “Pudput”, “Pulpud” and “Pulpite” in Latin, sometimes placed at Souk el-Obiod or Souk el-Abiod (Arabic: أبيض, or “white market”), was a colonia in the Roman province of Africa. It lies on the coast not far from the town of Hammamet and the modern town of Yasmine. (note: a Roman colonia / pl. coloniae was originally a settlement of Roman citizens which established a Roman base in federated or conquered territory in order to secure that territory. In the end, however, the term came to denote the highest status of a Roman town. It is also the origin of the modern word “colony”.) A large part of Pupput lies buried beneath modern holiday buildings, which were erected over much of the site. Beneath the resort where we were staying, too, there were the foundations of Roman baths. Of this I had no idea in the first few days, but on walks along the beach I kept finding fragments of terra sigillata sherds… I had already begun to suspect that it was some kind of mirage in the heat. After two days of lazing on a sun lounger and splashing about in the sea, I persuaded the family to set off on an exploration along the beach towards the more distant harbour. After 4 km of walking on the scorching sand under a blazing sun, over a cool drink in the harbour the majority voted to return to the resort by taxi… thanks to which I discovered that behind the high wall of our luxury there was an archaeological site… and what a site… I set off there with the words: “I am just going to have a look for 5 minutes…” but it took considerably longer. The town of Pupput – today’s Hammamet – lies in an agricultural region, densely inhabited above all in classical antiquity, though it was probably settled from the 5th century BC by Berbers and Carthaginians. Pupput was an important stop on the Roman road linking the cities of Carthage and Hadrumentum. Hadrumetum was a Phoenician colony that predated Carthage. It subsequently became one of the most important cities in Roman Africa, before the Vandal and Umayyad conquerors left it in ruins. In the early modern period it was the village of Hammeim. A number of Punic votive inscriptions, the so-called Punic stars, on stone stelae were found during excavations on the site of the modern Église Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception de Sousse, today part of Tunisian Sousse.

children.text: As early as the 1st century BC a settlement existed on the site where the town of Pupput later arose, which may have been of Berber-Punic origin. It was a simple vicus – a small village in Carthaginian territory at the time of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius (2nd century). It is assumed that the Roman politician Salvius Julianus was born in the village, and it may have been thanks to him that Pupput became an honorary colonia under the emperor Commodus (185–192). At that time the town was probably a satellite of its neighbour Neapolis. The earliest written mention of the town dates from 168, when it was raised to the status of a municipality governed by an elected council. It seems to have gained in importance during the 2nd and 3rd centuries, when it expanded considerably and a number of public buildings were erected. According to an inscription preserved in the Bardo National Museum in Tunis, which was dedicated to the 4th-century emperor Licinius, the Roman name of the town was “Colonia Aurelia Commoda Pia Felix Augusta Pupput”. In late antiquity the ancient town of Pupput would have become a vicus again. That did not happen, thanks to the fact that the episcopal see of Puppi arose here, corresponding to modern Souk-El-Abiodh south of Hammamet; it is listed in the episcopal lists of 411 (Donatists and Catholics), 484, 525 and 646. Puppi was the seat of an ancient Christian bishopric in the Roman province of Africa Proconsularis, a suffragan diocese of the archdiocese of Carthage. There are records of six bishops of the diocese of Puppi. Two of the bishops, the Catholic Pannonio and the Donatist Vittoriano, took part in the council of Carthage in 411, when Catholics and Donatists gathered to resolve the Donatist schism in Roman Africa. A third bishop, Aurelio, was a participant in the Council of Chalcedon in 451. Bishop Pastinato took part in the Vandal synod in Carthage in 484, which King Huneric convened in 484 in an attempt to persuade the Catholic bishops to convert to Arianism. After the synod Pastinato was exiled. Bishop Fortunato took part in the council of Carthage in 525, and Bishop Guloso took part in the council against the Monothelites in 646. In the Middle Ages, after the Vandal period, Pupput became part of the Byzantine Empire and a citadel was built for its defence. After the Arab conquest at the end of the seventh century the whole of Tunisia passed under Arab rule and the town was renamed Qasr Zaid. The town centre then shifted further to the north-east, where the town of Hammamet was founded, not far from the Roman baths, on the site of the medina. It seems that the ancient buildings of Souk el-Obiod were abandoned after this final relocation. Pirates from the kingdom of Aragon captured and destroyed the town in 1303 and left it in ruins. The area of Pupput was subsequently settled by charcoal burners from Hammamet. According to the friendly employee at the Pupput archaeological site, the meaning of the word Hammamet is: Hammam – one bath (singular), Hammamet – baths (plural). The archaeological site of Pupput is not much visited by crowds of tourists. The employee seemed very surprised at first when we came in and wanted to buy a ticket, but then enthusiasm and a kind of pride in the place got the better of him. He talked cheerfully about the archaeological excavation here on the spot and about the important historical points in the surroundings on the Mediterranean coast. I learned that the archaeological site is for the most part unexcavated. At present it is not protected in any way against the effects of the weather either. No professional archaeological excavation has taken place in the last 15 years or so, and in all likelihood no funds will be found in the coming period either for resuming the excavation or for protecting this cultural monument. Today what enchanted me here were the mosaics themselves, of a size I had not expected. The patterns of the mosaics on the floors were clear, the colours still bright despite the harsh sun, and the foundations of the baths, of the individual pools and rooms, legibly traced the separate parts of the building. In the grounds, beside the trees, stood huge amphorae for wine, olive oil and scented oils. Column capitals in the beautiful Corinthian style, part of a marble statue, decorated sections of walls, a stone bench in the shape of a lion… All of it spoke of the bygone beauty of this place - judge for yourselves from the photographs. At first sight this country is very poor, full of problems, and seems inhospitable, but Africa is not only about poverty, the burning sun and problems. Africa is a magical land full of surprising places, sweet fruit, the intoxicating scent of spices, history and extraordinary experiences. I could wander through these historical places for a very long time yet…
